title: WHAT IF YOU RODE A COMET
1.3 BILLION KM AWAY?

sets.comet: A comet in deep space. far: SpaceBackdrop #0A0A1E with sparse stars and slow light rays; mid: a dark lumpy grey-brown nucleus with pale ice patches and 4 px outline, with a bright cyan-white fuzzy coma around it and two long tails (a straight blue gas tail and a curved cream dust tail) streaming to the right; pale rim light. setp.t 0..1 = comet drifts left to right across the frame; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold' tints the coma; setp.jets 0..1 = streams of dust and gas spray from the nucleus.
sets.surface: Standing on the comet. near: a dark rough icy ground plane with cream-white ice patches, pale rim line; far: a huge black sky full of stars, a tiny bright Sun at the upper left, the long dust tail arching overhead. setp.t 0..1 = gas jets puff up from cracks in the ground; setp.tint 'dim'|'bright'.
sets.euclid: The Euclid space telescope in deep space. far: SpaceBackdrop with many tiny faint galaxies as soft smudges; mid: a boxy ESA telescope with a big round mirror barrel, a flat dark-blue sunshield and a small golden antenna, 4 px outline, pale rim light; setp.t 0..1 = slow drift; setp.stare 0..1 = a faint cyan cone widens from the telescope towards the sky; setp.blink 0|1 = a camera flash.
sets.frames: A sequence of telescope image frames. Deep-navy bg; five black square frames (cream 4 px borders) in a row, each speckled with tiny white stars; setp.t 0..1 = frames reveal one by one from left to right; setp.streak 0..1 = a short bright streak appears in each revealed frame at a slightly different spot, shifting along a dotted cream line; setp.fuzz 0..1 = the streak becomes a fuzzy cloud with a small bright dot.
sets.zoomframe: One big black telescope frame filling the screen with thousands of tiny stars and faint galaxy smudges; setp.t 0..1 = a small boxed region zooms in; setp.streak 0..1 = a smeared bright streak shows inside the box; setp.fuzz 0|1 = turns into a fuzzy comet dot with a soft halo; setp.ring 0|1 = cream circle highlights it.
sets.ops: Quiet office with a glowing monitor. far: wall of dark screens with soft cream charts; mid: a desk with a laptop and coffee mug, dark; near: carpet GroundPlane with pale rim. setp.alert 0..1 = the laptop screen flashes amber with a warning triangle; setp.ok 1 = screen turns green.
sets.catalog: A big dark catalogue screen: rows of cream text lines (comet and asteroid names) scrolling upward; setp.t 0..1 = a magnifier sweeps down the rows; setp.match 0|1 = 0 shows a red cross 'NO MATCH' stamp, 1 shows a green check; setp.scroll 0..1 = list scroll speed.
sets.mpc: Minor Planet Center alert. Deep-navy bg; a small globe of Earth dotted with cream pins at left, thin cream lines flying from one pin to others across the globe; setp.t 0..1 = alert lines spread to more pins; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.orbit: Top-down comet orbit. Deep-navy bg; a tiny yellow Sun at centre; small coloured planet dots on thin cream rings, outermost Jupiter and Saturn; a huge thin gold ellipse that goes far out beyond them; a bright comet dot on the ellipse. setp.t 0..1 = comet travels along the ellipse; setp.zoom 0..1 = zoom out (0 = inner planets, 1 = whole giant ellipse); setp.mark 0|1 = a pulsing cyan ring on the comet's current position.
sets.side: Side view of the Solar System. Deep-navy bg; a flat horizontal cream band with planets and the yellow Sun at left; a comet dot far above the band on a dotted gold line arching over; setp.t 0..1 = the dotted arch draws on; setp.up 0|1 = a cyan arrow points up from the Sun to the comet.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.
sets.sky: Looking up. A huge dark sky with the Milky Way band and many stars; near: a dark horizon line with tiny pale rim; setp.t 0..1 = a small fuzzy comet with a faint tail slowly rises; setp.glow 0..1 = brightness.

props.comet: Small comet icon: a lumpy grey nucleus with a bright cyan coma and a short two-colour tail, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props.euclid: Small ESA Euclid icon: boxy grey body with a round telescope barrel, flat dark-blue sunshield, tiny gold antenna; 4 px outline; pp.s scale.
props.frame: Small black square image frame with a cream 4 px border and a few white stars; pp.streak true adds a bright diagonal streak; pp.fuzz true makes it a fuzzy dot; pp.label text beneath.
props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.calendar: Small wall calendar page, cream with a red top strip, 4 px outline; pp.text the date in FONTS.title (max 8 chars).
props.magnifier: Outlined magnifying glass with a cream handle and pale glass; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a cyan bloom in the lens.
props.snowball: A round white-blue snowball icon with a dark 4 px outline, small pale sparkles; pp.s scale; pp.dirty true adds dark dust specks.
props.ring: Pulsing cyan circle outline, 4 px, soft bloom, that expands and fades each second; pp.s scale.

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back (headTilt up), arms hang loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms raised over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation (yaw/spin) across the shot while looking up.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point at the sky at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

film.vo: You are sitting on a comet. Nobody on Earth knew it existed.
It is one point three billion kilometres from home.
And a telescope that was not even looking for comets just found you.
A streak. A smudge. Then a brand new world on the map.
This happened this autumn. ESA's Euclid made the catch.
So what if you rode that comet?
You'd be going the long way round.
Here are the rules.
You hold on to the comet. You do not let go.
You bring nothing. Space has plenty of room for nothing.
Cold is fine. You're wearing your usual hoodie.
The trip is long. One lap takes thousands of years.
So pack patience. Lots of patience.
First, though, meet your ride.
A comet is a dirty snowball. Ice, dust and rock.
It is left over from the birth of the Solar System.
That was about four point six billion years ago.
So you are sitting on something truly ancient.
Most comets come from the far edge: the Kuiper Belt or Oort Cloud.
Out there it is dark, still and very cold.
Then the Sun warms a comet, and it wakes up.
Ice turns to gas. Gas drags dust. A fuzzy cloud blooms around you.
That cloud is the giveaway. It says this rock is active.
Hold that thought. The cloud is how they found you.
But who was looking? Nobody was.
Meet the one who was not looking.
Euclid is a European Space Agency telescope.
It launched in twenty twenty-three.
Its job is to stare at distant galaxies, slowly and deeply.
Long, steady pictures. Nothing fast. Nothing nearby.
Comets are fast and nearby. So, not its department.
On the sixteenth of September, Euclid starts taking pictures.
It keeps going until the twenty-fourth.
That is eight days of galaxies. And one passing stranger.
That stranger was you. Well, your comet.
It drifts across the shot like a fly across a window.
No one is watching live. The pictures just pile up.
Your comet could have slipped by unseen.
Until one person's software notices.
His name is Mikko Pöntinen, at the University of Helsinki.
He wrote a program to watch for small moving things.
It scans Euclid's pictures for streaks.
A streak means a fast mover smeared across several frames.
One day, it flags one.
He said, quote, I was excited to see my software flag a streak.
Now the hunt. Where does that streak go next?
He predicts its position. Then checks the other pictures.
It shows up again. And again.
Five separate image sets. Same object. Same path.
That's no glitch. Glitches do not move like that.
Then he zooms in on the dot.
And there it is. A fuzzy cloud around it.
Remember the cloud? Here is why it matters.
A plain rock would stay sharp. A fuzzy dot sheds dust and gas.
Fuzzy means active. Active means comet.
But is it new? Or has someone seen you before?
His team checks the catalogues of known comets and asteroids.
Row after row after row.
No match. You are not on any list.
That means you are brand new.
So Mikko reports it to the Minor Planet Center.
That's the group that keeps the official list.
The alert goes out. Telescopes on the ground can now take a look.
More eyes. More pictures. More proof.
On the eighth of October, it is official.
It is a comet. And it has a name.
Comet C slash twenty twenty-six S one. Euclid.
Euclid's very first new comet.
Now, where exactly are you sitting?
About one point three billion kilometres from Earth.
That is roughly between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.
Giants on both sides. Nobody around to wave to.
But you are not in the planets' flat lane.
The planets circle in one flat plane, like marbles on a table.
You are way above it. Straight up from the Sun.
Your path arches over the whole Solar System.
And one lap of that orbit takes thousands of years.
Whole civilisations would rise and fall. You would still be on lap one.

text.text: LAP ONE OF A LONG RACE

film.vo: Honestly, bring a book. Maybe several libraries.
You drift. The Sun is a long way back.
Dust and gas stream out behind you.
Out here, you are small, cold, and completely alone.
Here is the wild part. This find was luck.
Euclid avoids the crowded band where comets and asteroids live.
That band throws off dust glare. Glare ruins deep pictures.
But you were not in that band. You were straight up.
Also, Euclid works in a step-and-stare style.
It usually visits each patch of sky only once.
So no second look on demand.
Yet it caught you in several images over those days.
One scientist at ESA called it a happy coincidence.
The right orbit. The right days. The right software.
Miss any one of them and you stay hidden for years.
So did Euclid just give humanity a ride-along?
Not quite. ESA has a mission called Comet Interceptor.
It will fly to a comet that is still far from the Sun.
Your comet turned out not to be the right target.
But ESA called this a real test case.
Spot a comet, alert the world, and coordinate fast.
Two teams practised that dance on you.
One telescope. One program. Five lucky pictures.
And a brand new comet, one point three billion kilometres away.
Remember the very first line? You are sitting on a comet.

text.text: YOU ARE SITTING ON A COMET

film.vo: Now you know how a telescope, a coder and luck found you.
Tomorrow: what if the Sun switched off for one hour?
Which comet would you ride? Tell me below.

short.vo: You are sitting on a comet nobody knew existed.
It is one point three billion kilometres from Earth.
A telescope built for galaxies just spotted you.
It showed up in five separate image sets.
Around it, a fuzzy cloud of dust and gas.
No match in any catalogue. Brand new.
Confirmed on the eighth of October.
Meet comet C slash twenty twenty-six S one, Euclid.
You are between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.
Straight up from the Sun, on an orbit of thousands of years.
Euclid found it by happy coincidence.
Full film on the channel. Tomorrow: what if the Sun switched off?
